## A result that ran only once

Every quantitative health scientist has met the failure
this book exists to prevent. An analysis runs cleanly on
the machine where it was written and produces a table, a
figure, a p-value. A year later, on a new laptop, or a
colleague's, or a reviewer's, the same code errors, or
worse, runs to completion and returns a different number.
The statistics were sound. What failed was everything
around the statistics: a package that changed beneath the
code, a default that shifted between releases of R, a
system library present on one machine and absent on
another. The result had been reproducible exactly once, on
one machine, at one moment, and no one noticed until the
moment had passed.

This book is about closing that gap. Its subject is
computational reproducibility, by which we mean the
property that a computational result can be regenerated,
byte for byte or number for number, by another person on
another machine at a later time. That is a narrower claim
than scientific replication, and we shall be careful to
keep the two apart throughout. It is nonetheless a claim
that a great deal of published health-sciences research
cannot currently support. Unlike replication, it is also a
claim that can be secured by technical means available
today.

## What reproducibility means

The vocabulary of this field is contested, and a reader
should fix the terms before wading into the literature.
The National Academies, in their 2019 consensus report,
adopt a distinction we follow [@nas2019]. *Reproducibility*
is obtaining consistent computational results using the
same input data, computational steps, methods, code, and
conditions of analysis: it is a statement about
re-execution. *Replicability* is obtaining consistent
results across studies aimed at answering the same
question, each with its own data: it is a statement about
the robustness of a scientific finding. The two are
independent. A result can be perfectly reproducible and
entirely wrong, if the code faithfully regenerates a
mistaken number every time. Conversely, a finding can
replicate across laboratories while no single analysis in
the set is computationally reproducible. The point that a
reproducible analysis can still be wrong, and that
reproducibility is therefore a floor rather than a ceiling,
is pressed by Leek and Peng [@leek2015]. This book concerns
itself almost entirely with the first, and says so plainly
wherever the boundary is in doubt.

Reproducibility so defined is not a single threshold but a
spectrum. @peng2011 arranged computational work along a
scale from the merely published, through code available,
code and data available, and linked and executable, to
fully replicable. He argued that reproducibility is 'a
minimum standard for judging scientific claims when full
independent replication is impractical'. The lesson we take
from Peng, and develop into the levels ladder of
@sec-levels, is that reproducibility comes in degrees, and
that honesty about which degree one has reached is itself a
scientific virtue.

## The evidence that it is not happening

The case for taking this seriously is empirical, and it is
grim. In psychology, the Open Science Collaboration could
replicate only 39 of 100 studies it re-ran
[@opensciencecollaboration2015]. In preclinical oncology,
@begley2012 reproduced only 6 of 53 landmark findings.
These are replication failures, at the scientific end of
the spectrum, and their causes are many. But a growing body
of evidence isolates the specifically computational
failures, and they are, if anything, more damning because
they are more avoidable.

@trisovic2022, re-running more than nine thousand R files
deposited in the Harvard Dataverse, found that fewer than
one in four executed without error, even before asking
whether the output matched. @saju2025, examining R code
supplements on the Open Science Framework, found that only
about a quarter ran to completion, and that the vast
majority carried no description of their dependencies at
all. These are not analyses that reached the wrong
conclusion; they are analyses that could not be made to run
a second time. The scholarship, in Claerbout's phrase, was
advertised but never delivered.

Setting the four studies beside one another, as in
@fig-failure-rates, makes the shape of the problem visible.
The replication studies and the re-execution studies are
measuring different things, and the figure keeps them in
separate panels for that reason, but the rates are
comparably low in both. The difference that matters for
this book is that the right-hand panel counts failures that
no amount of additional data collection would fix, and that
better engineering would.

```{r}
#| label: fig-failure-rates
#| fig-cap: 'Reported success rates in four studies, separated by what each measured. The left panel reports replication studies, in which new data was collected to test a prior finding. The right panel reports re-execution studies, in which deposited code was run again without any attempt to evaluate the science. The re-execution figures are those stated in the text of the studies as cited in this chapter, and are approximate where the source reports a bound rather than a point estimate.'
#| fig-alt: 'A two-panel bar chart of four studies. The left panel, labeled replication, shows the Open Science Collaboration at 39 percent and Begley and Ellis at 11 percent. The right panel, labeled re-execution, shows Trisovic and colleagues at about 24 percent and Saju and colleagues at about 25 percent. All four bars sit well below half, and the two panels reach comparably low values by different routes.'
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2

library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

studies <- tibble(
  study = c('Open Science\nCollaboration (2015)',
            'Begley and\nEllis (2012)',
            'Trisovic et al.\n(2022)',
            'Saju et al.\n(2025)'),
  rate = c(39, 11, 24, 25),
  kind = factor(
    c('Replication: new data collected',
      'Replication: new data collected',
      'Re-execution: deposited code re-run',
      'Re-execution: deposited code re-run'),
    levels = c('Replication: new data collected',
               'Re-execution: deposited code re-run')
  )
)

ggplot(studies, aes(x = reorder(study, rate), y = rate)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = kind), width = 0.62, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(rate, '%')),
            hjust = -0.18, size = 3.4) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 48)) +
  facet_wrap(~kind, scales = 'free_y', ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    'Replication: new data collected' = '#4c72b0',
    'Re-execution: deposited code re-run' = '#14746f'
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = 'Reported success rate (percent)') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 8.5)
  )
```

## Why the failures are computational, not statistical

It is worth dwelling on why re-execution fails, because the
reasons point directly at the remedy. Consider two changes
to R itself, each silent and each capable of altering a
published result. In R 3.6.0 the default random-number
algorithm changed, so that code setting a seed and drawing
a sample obtained different draws before and after the
release, with no error and no warning. In R 4.0.0 the
`stringsAsFactors` default flipped from `TRUE` to `FALSE`,
so that code reading a data frame silently produced
character columns where it once produced factors. This
change in turn altered the behavior of every model that
treated those columns as categorical. Neither change was a bug; both were
improvements. Both would nonetheless break the exact
reproduction of an analysis written under the old default,
and neither would announce itself.

These are instances of a general phenomenon. A
computational result depends not only on the code and the
data but on a stack of determinants beneath them: the
operating system and its system libraries, the numerical
libraries that implement linear algebra, the language
runtime, the exact versions of every package, and the
session configuration. That configuration includes the
random-number kind, the contrasts, the number of printed
digits, and the locale and time zone. Underneath all of it
sits the hardware. A published script
pins almost none of these. It records the analysis logic
and, if the reader is fortunate, the data, and leaves the
remaining layers to whatever the next machine happens to
provide. Reproducibility fails in the gap between what the
script fixes and what the result depends on. The task of a
reproducibility toolchain is to close that gap, layer by
layer, and the organizing question of this book is how far
down the stack a given effort has actually reached.

## The tools, and the framework this book uses

The R ecosystem has, over two decades, produced mature
tools for nearly every layer of that stack. Literate
programming, `knitr`, R Markdown, and now Quarto
[@allaire2024], binds prose to the code that produces it.
`renv` [@ushey2020] pins package versions in a lockfile.
Docker, through Rocker's R-specific base images
[@boettiger2015; @nust2020rockerverse], pins the operating
system and its libraries. Continuous integration re-runs
the whole compendium on a clean machine to confirm that the
pinned layers actually suffice. Alternatives exist at every
layer, Nix and its R front-end `rix` in place of `renv`
[@dolstra2004; @rodrigues2024rix], Podman or Apptainer in
place of Docker [@kurtzer2017], GitLab in place of GitHub,
and this book introduces each tool where the chapter ahead
needs it rather than in one early catalog: @sec-dependencies
for package pinning, @sec-containers and @sec-backends for
the environment and its alternatives, @sec-compendium for
the compendium structure that @gentleman2007 and
@marwick2018's `rrtools` established, and @sec-pipelines,
@sec-testing, and @sec-verification for the workflow,
quality, and validation layer.

None of this tooling is the problem; composing it by hand
is. `renv` says nothing about the operating system, Docker
says nothing about which package versions are installed
inside it, and neither says anything about session
configuration, so a researcher who wants a genuinely
reproducible analysis must assemble all of it correctly,
for every project, by hand. This book's running example
uses `zzcollab`, a framework that assembles the triad,
`renv` for packages, Docker for the environment, continuous
integration for validation, into one coherent workflow, so
that a biostatistician obtains the composition without
building it from scratch. Each chapter ahead develops the
part of `zzcollab` relevant to its own layer against the
concept it has just introduced, rather than all at once
here.

Like every tool this book covers, `zzcollab` is held to the
standard it teaches. By its own accounting it firmly pins a
part of the [determinant stack](glossary.qmd#gloss-determinant-stack),
the environment, the
packages, the source, and the locale and time zone, and
leaves the rest, the numerical libraries, the random-number
discipline, the graphics device, intrinsic non-determinism,
to the base image or to convention. Reproducibility tooling
in general has an adoption problem more than a capability
problem: @saju2025 found that most deposited code
supplements carry no dependency description at all, even
though mature, free, documented tools for that exact
problem have existed for years. The book's task is
therefore less to invent than to make existing capability
teachable and routine, and to state plainly, at each level
of the ladder, what a given effort has secured and what
remains exposed, including its own.

## The plan of this book

The book is organized in four parts, and three ideas recur
in every chapter. It is written for a one-quarter, ten-week
course; not every chapter fits in ten weeks, and an
instructor teaching on that schedule should expect to treat
some material as optional. The first is the ladder of
reproducibility levels (L0 locatable, L1 pinned packages,
L2 pinned environment, L3 verified), introduced in
@sec-levels and used thereafter as the common scale. The
second is the distinction between capturing reproducibility
and validating it: pinning is capture, and continuous
integration and verification are validation. The third is
the research compendium as the unit of reproducible work,
introduced in @sec-compendium.

- **Part I, Foundations.** The reproducibility crisis and
  its computational character (@sec-crisis); the levels of
  reproducibility and the determinants that set them
  (@sec-levels); version control with git as the foundation
  of a locatable analysis (@sec-version-control); and the
  research compendium (@sec-compendium).
- **Part II, Capturing the environment.** Pinning packages
  with a lockfile (@sec-dependencies); pinning the operating
  system and runtime with a container (@sec-containers); and
  the alternatives, from Nix to Podman to Apptainer
  (@sec-backends).
- **Part III, Validation.** Literate programming and the
  rendered report (@sec-literate); automating the analysis
  with make and targets (@sec-pipelines); testing and code
  quality (@sec-testing); and continuous integration and
  verification (@sec-verification).
- **Part IV, Collaboration and stewardship.** Sharing a
  compendium with a team and with the world (@sec-archiving).

## How to use this book

The book is meant to be worked, not only read. Each chapter
develops a concept and then builds it, in R and at the
shell, inside a running example compendium. The reader who
follows along will finish with a reproducible project of
their own and, more durably, with the judgment to reason
about reproducibility with any toolchain and to state,
without flinching, the level a given analysis has actually
reached.

Seven habits recur across the chapters that follow, each a
concrete instinct rather than a slogan, and a chapter's own
rules of thumb will cite one by number rather than restate
it. The closing chapter recalls them once the book's
argument is complete.
